title: The Unsaid Glasshouse
premise: Sable Thornbury has spent fifteen years writing postcards to the glasshouse where she grew up—an address that burned down the night her foster brother, Idris, disappeared. When the estate is auctioned to fund a luxury development, Sable returns under a false name as the developer's hired archivist, cataloguing what survived the fire. Among the salvaged papers she finds letters in Idris's handwriting proving he didn't run away: he was sent away, by the one person Sable still loves. Confronting that truth—and the found family of neighbors who kept his secret to protect her—Sable must choose between preserving her invisibility and testifying at the auction hearing, which would finally speak the unsaid and claim both her name and her people.
about_author: Sable Quintana is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the paper trails of abandoned houses before turning to fiction. She writes from a coastal town where she keeps a postcard collection of buildings that no longer exist.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. We meet her precise, invisible life: the postcards to a burned address, the practiced smile, the rented room with no photographs. A letter arrives announcing the auction of Wrenfield House—the glasshouse estate—demanding any 'interested parties' come forward. She burns the letter, then unburns it from the ash. Emotional beat: the crack in a carefully sealed life.

chapters.title: Inventory of Ash
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Using her real credentials but a softened surname, she takes a contract job cataloguing the fire-salvaged contents for the developer, Halvard Voss. Walking the scorched glasshouse frame, she remembers nothing and everything. She pockets a child's marble without deciding to. Emotional beat: grief disguised as professionalism; the past asserting itself through objects.

chapters.title: The Neighbors Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, with dialogue-heavy scenes. The old neighborhood recognizes her despite the new name: Marisol the florist, deaf Mr. Okonkwo who reads lips through windows, teenage Theo who squats in the greenhouse ruins. Their warmth feels like surveillance. They know why she left; they won't say. Emotional beat: found family offered and distrusted.

chapters.title: What the Fire Kept
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. In a water-damaged trunk she finds Idris's letters—dated after his supposed disappearance—describing a 'placement' arranged by Aunt Corliss, the foster mother Sable worshipped. The letters stop mid-sentence. Sable lies to Voss about the trunk's contents. Emotional beat: vertigo; the foundation story of her life begins to tilt.

chapters.title: Voss's Blueprint
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Voss and Sable. Voss reveals the development will erase the glasshouse entirely, and offers Sable permanence—a job, an apartment, a place in his vision—if she certifies the archive as 'nothing of significance.' His charm is indistinguishable from coercion. Emotional beat: power seducing someone who has only ever known powerlessness.

chapters.title: Corliss, Alive
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She tracks Aunt Corliss to a care home two towns over. The reunion is tender and terrible: Corliss, lucid in flashes, admits she sent Idris away—to protect him from a man whose name she refuses to give, a man connected to the fire. She begs Sable to let the dead stay dead. Emotional beat: love and betrayal revealed as the same act.

chapters.title: The Marble
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The squatter teen has been finding things in the ruins too—including evidence someone set the fire deliberately, and a hiding place with more of Idris's belongings. He confronts Sable, angry that she'll leave again like everyone does. She gives him the marble; he gives her the hiding place. Emotional beat: reluctant kinship; the found family tightening whether she consents or not.

chapters.title: The Man from the Placement Office
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Following Corliss's half-name, Sable uncovers Garrick Hale—now a planning commissioner with authority over the very auction of Wrenfield House, the man who placed Idris in an institution and burned the records. He recognizes her at a public hearing and smiles her own smile back at her. Emotional beat: rising dread; the powerful closing ranks around their crime.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax, multiple POVs converging at the auction hearing. Voss demands Sable certify the archive; Hale expects her silence; the neighbors arrive uninvited with the letters, the marble, Theo's photographs of the ruins. Sable stands, drops her false name, and speaks Idris's full name into the record—naming Hale, naming the fire, naming herself. Emotional beat: the unsaid said; identity claimed at maximum cost.

chapters.title: Glasshouse, Replanted
chapters.summary: Resolution, Sable's POV. The development is halted pending investigation; the glasshouse will become a community archive run by Marisol, Okonkwo, and Theo—with Sable's name on the founding papers. She visits Corliss, bringing not forgiveness yet but presence. She writes one last postcard to the burned address and mails it to herself instead. Emotional beat: quiet, earned belonging; the invisible woman, visible at last.
